segments.text: {26th|Twenty-sixth} of January, {1972|nineteen seventy-two}. A passenger jet breaks apart ten kilometres above Czechoslovakia. One flight attendant falls all the way to the ground, with no parachute.
She lives. And ten months later, she walks.
No chance. Nobody falls ten kilometres and lives. Let's go look.

Belgrade, {1971|nineteen seventy-one}. Vesna {Vulović|Voolovitch} is twenty-one and loves the Beatles. One day she sees a friend in an air hostess uniform, and she applies to the national airline, {JAT|Jat}.

One problem. She has low blood pressure, and she is afraid the airline medical will fail her. So, by her own account, she drinks a great deal of coffee before the exam. She passes. Remember the coffee.

January {1972|nineteen seventy-two}. The airline needs a crew for Flight {367|three six seven}, and it rosters a flight attendant called Vesna. The wrong Vesna. She is not even meant to be on this flight.
Her crew takes the plane over in Copenhagen. A DC-9, on its way from Stockholm to Belgrade. At a quarter past three it takes off, with {28|twenty-eight} people on board.
{46|Forty-six} minutes later it is cruising over Czechoslovakia, {10,160|ten thousand one hundred and sixty} metres up.
At one minute past four, a bomb goes off in the forward baggage hold. The jet comes apart in the air.
{27|Twenty-seven} passengers and crew are killed. I have nothing clever to say about that.
Vesna is inside a torn-off section of the fuselage. A food trolley has pinned her in place, so she is not pulled out into the sky.
And here is the coffee. Doctors later told her that her low blood pressure made her pass out fast when the cabin lost pressure, and that this kept her heart from bursting on impact.
The section falls ten thousand metres, and comes down at an angle on a steep, wooded hillside, deep in snow. The trees and the snow take some of the blow.
Near the village of Srbská Kamenice, a man called Bruno Honke reaches the wreck. And he hears someone screaming inside.
Honke was a medic in the Second World War. He knows what to do, and he keeps her alive until the rescuers get there.
A fractured skull. Three broken vertebrae. Both legs broken. She is paralysed from the waist down, and she is in a coma.
Then she wakes up. And the first thing she asks for is a cigarette.

She remembers nothing of the explosion or the fall. So in March, when they fly her home to Belgrade and offer her something to help her sleep on the plane, she says no. She has no memory of a crash to be afraid of.
The feeling in her legs comes back. Within ten months she is walking again, with a limp she keeps for life.
Then she asks for her old job back. The airline says no to the sky, and gives her a desk, negotiating freight contracts.
In {1985|nineteen eighty-five}, Guinness puts her in its hall of fame. The highest fall survived without a parachute. And the man who hands her the medal is Paul McCartney. A Beatle.
And the bomb? The day after, a man phoned a Swedish newspaper, called himself a Croatian nationalist, and claimed it. Nobody was ever arrested.

In {2009|two thousand and nine}, two journalists argued that the jet had been far lower, and was shot down by mistake. The Czech aviation authority dismissed it, and the journalists called their own evidence circumstantial. The record still stands.
Vesna lost that desk job in the early nineties, after speaking out against Slobodan {Milošević|Miloshevitch}. She died in Belgrade in December {2016|twenty sixteen}, aged {66|sixty-six}.
I said nobody falls ten kilometres and lives. One person did. I was wrong. Case closed.
